doc.title: Yusef Lateef — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Why he moved beyond standard forms and world music reaction
summary: He explains he could not keep writing on I Got Rhythm and needed new forms and instrumentation to avoid monotony.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I’m fine. Okay. Okay. Oh, just looking, looking at the uh, beginning with your first recording, your uh, your interest in what has been dubbed, and, and I use this apologetically, uh “world music” long before this term was even fashioned.

Uh it brings to mind one of the, the core questions for the interview regarding critical response to this. What...–because as, as we uh look at the history of the music now, it’s clear that people like yourself and, and, and, you know, later Don Cherry and people like that, were looking beyond uh, or in addition to what was found here at other,
the music and, and rhythmic and melodic contributions of other cultures–what was the critical response to uh, to your, your early efforts along this line?

Well, like I said, I felt if, if I would continue to record I’d have to, I couldn’t give the people the same thing over and over. I mean, I felt that...like you can right a song based on I Got Rhythm, you know, like Moose the Mooche....

...[indecipherable], you know. But how many times, how many tunes can you write on I Got Rhythm before it...it becomes redundant to oneself? Um so I thought I had to change that–the form, the instrumentation–in order to avoid monotony. I mean, you take people like Charlie Parker and Sonny Stitt, they got all the juice out the blues and I Got Rhythm. That was their offering, you know?
They were masters at that. So, I figured I had to find my own expression, like they had.
